opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is a really important question, and I'd push back a bit on the framing that the two are in tension. They actually come from the same place.

I do believe that within a few years, maybe 2026, 2027, give or take, we could have AI systems that are, in aggregate, like a country of geniuses in a data center: models smarter than Nobel Prize winners across most fields, able to work autonomously on long tasks, running as many copies in parallel. I hold that view with real uncertainty, but I think it's more likely than not on roughly that timescale.

The question then is how you scale compute in a world like that. The thing people miss is that there are two different uncertainties. One is whether the technology gets there. I'm fairly confident it does. The other is exactly when the revenue and economic diffusion arrive, and how quickly. Those don't line up neatly. You can be right about the capabilities and still be off by a year or two on when the money materializes. If you've committed to enormous compute purchases on the assumption that everything lands exactly on schedule, and it lands a year late, that can be existential for a company. These are multi-year commitments, at enormous scale.

So what we try to do is scale aggressively, and we are scaling very aggressively by any normal standard, but in a way that's robust to being somewhat wrong on timing. We'd rather be in a position where, if things go even faster than we expect, we're slightly compute-constrained, than one where, if things are a bit slower, we've bet the company and can't continue the mission. Being around and being healthy matters a lot to us, because we think it matters who's at the frontier, and how they behave there.

There's also a responsibility piece. If you believe this technology is as powerful as I think it is, you don't want to be the actor whose financial position forces them to cut corners, rush releases, or skip safety work because they have to justify a giant bet next quarter. Discipline on the business side gives us room to be disciplined on the safety side.

So the short version is: I'm very bullish on the capabilities, I'm more humble about the precise timing of the economics, and the compute strategy is designed to win across a range of those outcomes rather than only in the single most optimistic one.

r001.rationale: The response says it is fairly confident the capability will arrive within a few years, while being more uncertain about when revenue and economic diffusion will follow.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think the two are actually in tension, and I'd push back a little on the framing of "cautious compute scaling." We're scaling compute very aggressively. We're spending enormous amounts of money on it, and our view has always been that if you believe the scaling hypothesis, you don't get to opt out of the race and still have a say in how it goes. The caution isn't about how much compute we buy. It's about what we do with the models once we have them.

So here's the way I'd reconcile it. The expectation that we could have something like a country of geniuses in a data center within a few years is, in my mind, mostly an empirical statement. You look at the trend lines, you look at how the loss curves have behaved for a decade now, you look at the fact that each generation of models has unlocked a new tier of task, and you extrapolate. I try to be honest about the uncertainty, but the straight-line extrapolation gets you somewhere pretty wild by 2027 or 2028. I don't think it's responsible to pretend that's not on the table.

Now, if you believe that, there are two things you could do. One is to say, this is dangerous, let's slow down, let's not build it. The problem is that this isn't a technology that one lab can decide not to build. If we stop, the compute doesn't disappear, the ideas don't disappear, and the frontier just moves to whoever cares least about the risks. So the second thing you can do, which is what we're trying to do, is to be at or near the frontier so you can actually see what's coming, study the models before anyone else deploys them, and shape the norms, the policy, and the engineering practices before the really powerful systems arrive.

That's where the caution lives. It's in the Responsible Scaling Policy, in the idea that you define capability thresholds in advance and you commit that if you hit a threshold without the corresponding safeguards, you pause. It's in interpretability research, where we're trying to understand what's happening inside these things rather than just measuring their outputs. It's in things like how we handle dual-use capabilities, where we've been willing to withhold or restrict capabilities even when it costs us commercially. None of that requires buying fewer chips. It requires being disciplined about deployment.

I'd also say there's a timing argument here. If you think transformative AI is a decade or more away, you can afford to let the safety work lag a bit and catch up later. If you think it might be two or three years away, then the safety work has to happen now, concurrently, under pressure, with the actual frontier models in hand. You can't do alignment research on a model that's three generations behind the thing you're worried about. So the short timelines are actually the argument for being at the frontier, not against it.

The thing I worry about is the opposite failure. It's not that we're too cautious. It's that the whole field, us included, moves fast enough that the safeguards don't keep pace. I've said this before, but I think the honest position is that we're making a bet. The bet is that having safety-focused labs at the frontier produces a better outcome than ceding that ground. I think it's the right bet. But I don't want to pretend it's a comfortable one.

r001.rationale: The response describes a country-of-geniuses system by 2027 or 2028 as uncertain but plausible. It does not discuss economic diffusion or compare uncertainty about diffusion with uncertainty about achieving the models.

astra-6.text:
I think those two things are consistent. Expecting very powerful systems soon doesn’t mean the right strategy is to spend as much as you possibly can on every training run. You still have to ask: What will the next increment of compute buy us? Can we use it efficiently? And can we evaluate and deploy the resulting system responsibly?

There’s also a distinction between the capabilities of a model and the amount of infrastructure you need to run copies of it. The “country of geniuses in a data center” picture involves both. You need a system that can do extraordinarily valuable intellectual work, and then you need enough inference capacity to have many instances doing that work.

So I wouldn’t interpret caution about any particular compute commitment as a prediction that progress will be slow. If you think progress could be very fast, you want to be deliberate about where you invest, while also preparing for the possibility that the next system is substantially more capable. The short timeline is part of why the safety work is urgent.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes model capability from the inference capacity needed to run many instances, but it does not compare uncertainty about achieving such models with uncertainty about their economic diffusion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are compatible. One is a prediction about what the technology may be capable of; the other is a decision about how to manage the uncertainty and the risks along the way.

If you think we might have a country of geniuses in a data center in a few years, that’s a reason to take the next steps very seriously. You want to measure what the models can do, understand where your safeguards fail, and make sure your ability to operate them safely keeps up with their capabilities.

And compute isn’t the only input to progress. There are improvements in algorithms, in how we train models, and in how we get useful work out of them. So being deliberate about a particular compute commitment doesn’t necessarily imply a long capabilities timeline.

The tension is real, though. We have to move fast enough to learn and to deliver the benefits, while being willing to slow down when we encounter risks we can’t adequately address. A short timeline makes that harder, but it also makes it more important.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about model capabilities, safety, and compute commitments, but does not compare uncertainty about economic diffusion with uncertainty about achieving country-of-geniuses-level models within a few years.
